messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Fashion Designer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 41

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me, Avoid Dreams: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares, Self-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what I have done wrong
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Memory: No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Arthur Vance had spent decades convincing himself that his temperament was fundamentally broken, a conviction that first took root in the years following his father’s escalating rages. Believing himself permanently changed for the worse by the childhood abuse, he stopped allowing himself to process the past and instead fell into a cycle of dwelling on what his father had done, then punishing himself for what he believed he had done wrong to deserve it. This rigid mental habit became his only way to navigate loss of control, anchoring his daily existence in a loop of resentment and self-reproach. That same conviction warped how his body read the present. Because he was certain people could not be trusted, any unannounced contact—like a tailor’s measuring tape snapping near his ribs or a colleague’s hand landing on his shoulder at the pattern-cutting table—triggered a jolt of pure alarm that left his breath catching and his shoulders locking. His distrust did not stay abstract; it manifested as a physical startle that made collaboration nearly impossible in his Greenwich Village studio. His fractured worldview also dictated how the past arrived in his mind. Convinced that his nervous system was broken beyond repair, Arthur found that when memories surfaced, they refused to cohere into a linear timeline; instead, they shattered into disjointed fragments he could never piece together, leaving him unable to tell a clear story of what happened even to himself. The lack of narrative structure felt like proof that his mind was simply failing him. Those fragmented recollections, in turn, flooded his workspace with phantom warnings. When a sudden draft silenced the hum of his industrial sewing machines, the empty quiet would pull the disjointed memories forward, and his body would immediately tense, convinced that something dangerous was about to happen. The memories did not just return; they hijacked his present-moment safety. The terror of those unspooling memories reinforced his core beliefs about his own deterioration. Every time he stared at a photograph and felt a hollow, numb detachment—as if watching a stranger’s life unfold on a screen—his inability to feel the expected grief or anger confirmed his fear that he was losing his grip on reality. His own physiological state then scrambled his ability to access the past at all. The constant readiness to bolt whenever his posture went rigid meant that any attempt to review old journals was met with a wall of panic, leaving him unable to retrieve or integrate the events without his thoughts fracturing further. That relentless readiness also cemented his worst interpretations. The way his heart hammered against his ribs whenever he stood alone in his now-empty loft convinced him that his own body was plotting against him, teaching him to view his nervous system not as an overprotective alarm, but as a traitor confirming his permanent damage. His relentless rumination, meanwhile, eroded his capacity to make sense of what occurred. By obsessively replaying arguments with his stepfather and his own perceived childhood failures, Arthur drowned out the few coherent details that might have emerged, ensuring that his trauma remained a tangled knot rather than a processed memory. Finally, this endless mental circling solidified his despair. When he exhausted himself analyzing the violence he survived, the emotional hangover left him certain that he was beyond repair, transforming temporary distress into a fixed belief that his reactions since the event meant he was going crazy. Arthur Vance is a fifty-five-year-old fashion designer whose once-bustling atelier now sits half-finished, garments draped over mannequins like unspoken accusations. Over the past two years, the combination of avoiding bed and sleepless nights, coupled with feeling on guard even inside his own home, has bled into his livelihood. He now refuses to work after dusk, claiming the twilight makes his nerves twitch, and he has fired three assistants who tried to hand him tools without verbal warning. Divorced and isolated, he was finally driven to seek help after a recent fitting: when a client reached out to touch his wrist, Arthur recoiled so violently he knocked over a rack of silk bolts. The sudden guilt on recall when the memories briefly broke through had been paralyzing. He came to my office hoping to stop the panic attacks and quiet the relentless loops in his head, terrified that if he stops fighting the memories, he will finally lose his mind entirely.
